hints: Compare the particles present: a lattice of identical metal atoms and delocalised electrons versus oppositely charged ions from a metal and a non-metal.
walkthrough:
Sort by particle type**
Picture magnesium first. It is a pure metal, so you have $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. That picture is always metallic bonding. Now picture sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$. You have a metal transferring electrons to a non-metal to give $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions in a giant lattice. That is ionic bonding.

Final answer: Bonding in magnesium: metallic
Bonding in sodium chloride: ionic

hints: Both solids have high melting points because both have strong giant structures, so focus on which set of attractions needs more thermal energy to break, using the data 923 K versus 1074 K.
walkthrough:
Link melting point to bond strength**
Melting loosens a giant structure. The higher the melting point, the stronger the attractions you must overcome. $\text{NaCl}$ melts at 1074 K, higher than Mg at 923 K, so its bonding must be stronger overall.

State the comparison clearly**
Both have strong bonding, but the ionic attractions between $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions in the giant ionic lattice are stronger than the metallic attraction between $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions and delocalised electrons. That is why $\text{NaCl}$ needs more heat to melt.
Final answer: Ionic bonds in $\text{NaCl}$ are stronger than metallic bonds in $\text{Mg}$, so more energy is needed to break them and melting point is higher.

hints: Recall that solid phosphorus ($\text{P}_4$) and sulfur ($\text{S}_8$) are both simple molecular lattices, so melting only overcomes weak intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.
Compare the size of the molecules in terms of total electrons and how easily their electron clouds can form temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
Check what is actually melting**
Do not be tricked into talking about breaking covalent bonds. Phosphorus exists as $\text{P}_4$ molecules and sulfur as $\text{S}_8$ molecules. Both form simple molecular lattices. On melting, the strong P-P and S-S covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact. You only separate molecules, so you only break weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.

Count electrons to compare force strength**
An $\text{S}_8$ molecule has $8 \times 16 = 128$ electrons, while a $\text{P}_4$ molecule has $4 \times 15 = 60$ electrons. The larger electron cloud in $\text{S}_8$ is more easily polarised, so it forms stronger temporary dipoles.

Connect to melting point**
Stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between $\text{S}_8$ molecules need more thermal energy to overcome than those between $\text{P}_4$ molecules. That is why sulfur melts at 392 K, higher than phosphorus at 317 K.

Final answer: $\text{S}_8$ molecules have more electrons than $\text{P}_4$ molecules.
Therefore sulfur has stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between molecules, requiring more energy to overcome, so higher melting point.

hints: Think of the word parts: electro for electrons and negativity for pulling power, and remember it refers to a bonded atom, not an isolated ion.
walkthrough:
Learn the exact phrase**
Electronegativity is about tug of war for a shared pair. Picture two atoms sharing electrons in a covalent bond. Electronegativity measures how strongly one atom pulls that shared pair towards itself. You must include the idea of a covalent bond to get the mark.
Final answer: The power of an atom to attract electrons to itself in a covalent bond.

hints: List what changes across a period from left to right: number of protons, number of shells, and approximate shielding.
Think how the pull felt by a bonding pair changes when nuclear charge rises but distance and shielding stay almost the same.
walkthrough:
Track protons and shells**
Move left to right across a period. Each step adds one proton to the nucleus, so nuclear charge rises. Electrons are added to the same shell, so extra shielding is very small and atomic size actually shrinks a little.

Feel the stronger pull**
With more protons pulling and almost no extra shielding to block them, the effective nuclear attraction on the outer shell and on any bonding pair increases. The nucleus tugs shared electrons closer.

Give the trend**
Because the bonding electrons are more strongly attracted to the nucleus, the power to attract electrons in a bond rises. That is why electronegativity increases across a period.

Final answer: Across a period nuclear charge increases with similar shielding / same number of shells.
Atomic radius decreases so bonding electrons are more strongly attracted to the nucleus, so electronegativity increases.

hints: Check for the hydrogen bond recipe in $\text{NH}_3$: H attached to N plus a lone pair on N of a neighbour.
walkthrough:
Spot the hydrogen bond conditions**
Look at $\text{NH}_3$. Hydrogen is directly bonded to very electronegative nitrogen, giving a $\delta+ \text{H}$, and nitrogen carries a lone pair. When another $\text{NH}_3$ approaches, that lone pair attracts the $\delta+ \text{H}$. That special strong dipole attraction is hydrogen bonding, the strongest intermolecular force here.
Final answer: Hydrogen bond / hydrogen bonding

hints: Sketch two pyramidal $\text{NH}_3$ molecules side by side, showing N with its lone pair and three N-H bonds on each.
Decide where the dashed H-bond line must go and which atoms need $\delta-$ and $\delta+$ labels to show the dipole attraction.
walkthrough:
Draw two ammonia molecules correctly**
Draw two separate $\text{NH}_3$ units. Each N has three single bonds to H and one lone pair. Show that lone pair clearly as two dots on N, because it is the acceptor.

Add the hydrogen bond in the right place**
Join them with a dashed line, not a solid covalent bond. The line must run from the lone pair on N of one molecule to an H atom of the other molecule: $\text{N}: --- \text{H}-\text{N}$. This shows the lone pair to $\delta+ \text{H}$ attraction.

Label the dipoles**
Because N is more electronegative than H, label N as $\delta-$ and H as $\delta+$. You need at least three correct labels across the two molecules, for example $\delta-\text{N}-\delta+\text{H}---\delta-\text{N}$. Those charges prove you understand why the H-bond forms.

Final answer: Diagram showing: $\text{H}_3\text{N}---\text{H}-\text{NH}_2$ with H-bond as dashed line from lone pair on N of one $\text{NH}_3$ to H of the other $\text{NH}_3$.
Minimum three correct partial charges shown, e.g. $\delta-\text{N}-\delta+\text{H}---\delta-\text{N}$ or $\delta+\text{H}---\delta-\text{N}-\delta+\text{H}$, with lone pair on N involved in H-bond.

hints: Compare the polarity of O-H versus N-H by recalling the relative electronegativity of O and N.
Count how many H-bonds each molecule can form on average by looking at lone pairs and H atoms: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has two of each, $\text{NH}_3$ has one H-bond donor effectively in the liquid.
walkthrough:
Compare bond polarity**
Both ice and ammonia use hydrogen bonding, but not equally strong. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the O-H bond is more polar than N-H. The $\text{H}$ is more $\delta+$ and the O is more $\delta-$, giving a stronger dipole attraction and a stronger hydrogen bond in water.

Count bonds per molecule**
Now count how many bonds hold the liquid together. Each $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ can form on average two hydrogen bonds per molecule, using its two H atoms and two lone pairs. Each $\text{NH}_3$ forms on average only one hydrogen bond per molecule in the liquid. More bonds per molecule plus stronger individual bonds means much more thermal energy is needed to melt ice, so ice melts at 273 K versus 195 K for ammonia.

Final answer: O is more electronegative than N, so O-H hydrogen bonds are stronger / more polar than N-H hydrogen bonds.
Water forms on average two H-bonds per molecule whereas ammonia forms one per molecule, so more energy needed to separate water molecules.
